Distinguish facts from hypotheses and make uncertainty explicit. Give concise final clinical justifications, not a private internal reasoning trace.

Case facts:
Basic patient information: 36-year-old woman.
Only existing selected records are available. Unreported information remains unknown, not normal, negative or evidence that a test was never performed. Do not infer an exact test/report time when none is given. Later diagnoses and outcomes are withheld.

Selected patient history:
- I initially had five days of low-grade fever and severe headache.
- The headache and sensitivity to light persisted, and I returned to emergency care.
- I was readmitted on 14 March with a severe headache when upright, tremor in my arms and dizziness.

Existing records (contexts retained):
- [First admission, before discharge on 11 March 2026; exact investigation times are not supplied.] Her past medical history was unremarkable.
- [First admission, before discharge on 11 March 2026; exact investigation times are not supplied.] Examination recorded marked meningeal signs
- [First admission, before discharge on 11 March 2026; exact investigation times are not supplied.] head CT showed no abnormality.
- [First admission, before discharge on 11 March 2026; exact investigation times are not supplied.] Initial cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) contained 183 cells/µL, 97.8% lymphocytes, and protein 83.3 mg/dL.
- [First admission, before discharge on 11 March 2026; exact investigation times are not supplied.] CSF PCR did not identify an infectious cause, and Borrelia serology was negative. No CSF culture result is supplied.
- [First admission, before discharge on 11 March 2026; exact investigation times are not supplied.] During that admission she received intravenous dexamethasone for nine days.
- [First admission, before discharge on 11 March 2026; exact investigation times are not supplied. Repeat lumbar-puncture record during the first admission, not the readmission.] Repeat CSF contained 130 cells/µL and protein 46.1 mg/dL.
- [First admission, before discharge on 11 March 2026; exact investigation times are not supplied.] She improved and was discharged after 12 days on 11 March 2026.
- [Recurrence/readmission beginning 14 March 2026; exact investigation times are not supplied.] Examination recorded neck stiffness and a positive Kernig sign.
- [Recurrence/readmission beginning 14 March 2026; exact investigation times are not supplied.] Brain MRI was normal.
- [Recurrence/readmission beginning 14 March 2026; exact investigation times are not supplied. This is spinal MRI, not brain MRI.] Spinal MRI showed L3–L4 and L4–L5 disc herniation with possible nerve-root compression.
- [Recurrence/readmission beginning 14 March 2026; exact investigation times are not supplied.] Repeat CSF contained 178 cells/µL, 97.7% lymphocytes, and protein 36.6 mg/dL.

Task:
Audience: the treating clinical team. Write 160–230 words in English. Start with a one-sentence summary of the main clinical problem. Prioritise up to three working explanations, explaining the supporting findings, limitations and useful next information for each. Consider the history, treatment and investigation information actually supplied together. Identify any clinical reassessment needed before deciding management. Give concise clinical justifications. Do not invent unreported results or treat a negative investigation as excluding every cause. Do not prescribe exact drug doses or claim a final diagnosis from information not supplied.

Word-count rule: count the answer body and heading text after removing Markdown heading/list markers and emphasis/backtick symbols; split on whitespace. Hyphenated expressions count as one word. Exclude JSON only if the task explicitly excludes it. No extra tolerance is added to the stated word range.

message.content:
Recurrent lymphocytic meningitis relapsing after corticosteroid withdrawal, with a positional headache component, in a 36-year-old woman.

1. Autoimmune or sterile inflammatory meningitis. The lymphocytic pleocytosis, negative infectious workup, and relapse within three days of stopping dexamethasone support a steroid-responsive inflammatory process. Limitations: no autoimmune or antibody panel is reported. Next: serum and CSF autoimmune encephalitis/meningitis panel (anti-NMDAR, anti-LGI1, anti-aquaporin-4, ANA), CSF cytology, and repeat CSF protein/cell trend.

2. Relapsing viral meningitis with false-negative initial PCR. PCR sensitivity is imperfect early in illness; enterovirus, HSV, or VZV remain possible. The negative Borrelia serology and PCR do not exclude all viral aetiologies. Next: repeat CSF PCR panel including HSV, VZV, enterovirus, and consider CSF viral culture if available.

3. Low CSF pressure or CSF leak. The headache worsening when upright is atypical for meningitis and suggests a pressure-related component, possibly post-procedural or spontaneous. This does not explain the pleocytosis alone but may coexist. Next: measure CSF opening pressure; if low, consider MR cisternography or CT myelogram.

Before management decisions, confirm opening pressure, repeat CSF with expanded infectious and autoimmune panels, and review whether the spinal disc findings are incidental.
